Trying to Conceive

Understanding Your Menstrual Cycle and Fertile Window

Updated: July 1, 2026

This article is shown in English while its translation is prepared.

Knowing how your cycle works is the single most useful skill when you are trying to conceive. It tells you when you are most likely to get pregnant — your fertile window — so you can focus your efforts on the right days.

The phases of the menstrual cycle

A cycle is counted from the first day of one period to the first day of the next. It has two main phases: the follicular phase (from your period until ovulation) and the luteal phase (from ovulation until your next period).

The average cycle is about 28 days, but anywhere from roughly 21 to 35 days is common. The luteal phase is fairly consistent at about 12–14 days, while the follicular phase varies more from person to person.

What is ovulation?

Ovulation is when an ovary releases a mature egg. It typically happens about 12–16 days before your next period starts — not necessarily on "day 14," which is a common misconception for anyone whose cycle is not exactly 28 days.

Once released, the egg survives for around 12–24 hours. If it is not fertilized in that time, the cycle moves toward your next period.

Your fertile window

Because sperm can survive in the reproductive tract for up to about five days, your fertile window spans roughly the five days before ovulation plus the day of ovulation itself — about six days total.

The two to three days leading up to and including ovulation are the most fertile. Having intercourse during this window gives sperm the best chance of meeting the egg.

How to estimate when you ovulate

If your cycles are regular, subtract about 14 days from your expected next period to estimate ovulation. Tracking a few cycles reveals your personal pattern.

Body signs help too: cervical mucus becomes clear and stretchy (like raw egg white) near ovulation, and basal body temperature rises slightly just after. Ovulation predictor kits detect the hormone surge that precedes ovulation.

When cycles are irregular

Irregular or unpredictable cycles make the fertile window harder to pin down and can sometimes signal an underlying issue worth checking. Tracking signs like mucus and temperature is especially helpful here.

If your cycles are very irregular, very short, or very long, or you have been trying without success, it is reasonable to speak with a healthcare provider.

Key takeaways

  • A cycle runs from the first day of one period to the first day of the next.
  • Ovulation usually happens about 12–16 days before your next period, not always day 14.
  • The fertile window is roughly the 5 days before ovulation plus ovulation day.
  • Cervical mucus, temperature, and ovulation kits help pinpoint the window.
  • Very irregular cycles are worth discussing with a provider.

Frequently asked questions

Can I get pregnant on any day of my cycle?

Pregnancy is only possible around ovulation, but because sperm live for several days, intercourse in the days before ovulation can still lead to conception. Timing outside the fertile window is very unlikely to result in pregnancy.

How often should we have intercourse when trying?

Every one to two days during the fertile window is a common recommendation. Regular intercourse across the window removes the pressure of hitting one exact day.

Is a 28-day cycle "normal"?

It is average, but cycles from about 21 to 35 days are considered normal. What matters more is that your cycles are reasonably regular for you.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
